planting.note: Start seed indoors 10-12 weeks before the last frost and transplant pencil-thick seedlings out for a late-season crop that will stand through winter.

directions: Bandit is an open-pollinated late-season leek bred for standing through hard freezes without splitting or losing quality, making it a favorite for gardeners who want fresh leeks well into winter rather than a single fall harvest. Trench or hill soil around the dark blue-green shanks as they grow to lengthen and blanch the edible white portion, since this variety produces very little natural bulbing and stays uniformly thick and straight. Keep plants weeded and evenly watered through summer so the stalks bulk up before cold weather triggers the hardiness that lets Bandit sit in the garden, unharvested, through repeated freezes. Choose Bandit over early-season leeks when the goal is a reliable, cold-tolerant crop to pull as needed from November through late winter.

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into fertile soil for an early-maturing, high-yield fall crop.

directions: Megaton is a vigorous F1 hybrid leek grown for its exceptional uniformity and speed to maturity compared with older open-pollinated types, producing long, thick, upright shanks under wide dark green leaves. Its hybrid vigor means less outer-leaf cleaning is needed at harvest to reveal a straight, market-ready stalk, which makes it popular with growers who sell bunched leeks. Give plants rich, consistently moist soil and hill soil around the base as they thicken to extend the blanched white shank. Because Megaton matures earlier than winter-hardy heirloom leeks, it suits gardeners wanting a heavy early-to-mid fall harvest rather than a leek held in the ground through deep winter.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost; this large-growing heirloom needs a long season to bulk up before harvest.

directions: Prizetaker, also sold as Lyon Prizetaker, is an English heirloom leek dating to the 1880s that was bred for exhibition size, producing some of the thickest, tallest shanks of any leek variety while staying remarkably tender for its bulk. Give it wide spacing and rich, deeply worked soil so roots have room to support the plant's large stature, and hill soil progressively around the base through the season to blanch a long white shank. Its dark green leaves and pure white, solid base have made it a favorite for county-fair and garden-show exhibitors for over a century, but it performs equally well as a substantial main-season leek for the kitchen. Because it needs a long growing season to reach full size, start it early and expect a later harvest than quick early-season types.

planting.note: Plant shallot sets 4-8 weeks before the last frost in spring, or in fall in zones 7-10 for a heavier early-summer crop.

directions: Longor is a traditional French shallot valued for producing unusually long, slender bulbs with coppery skin and pink-tinged flesh, distinguishing it from the rounder Dutch-type shallots grown for the fresh market. Plant sets shallow with the tip just showing above the soil surface and keep the bed weed-free, since each set divides into a cluster of several elongated bulbs by midsummer. Reduce watering once foliage begins to yellow and topple, then lift, dry, and cure the bulbs in a warm, airy spot before storing. Longor is prized in French cooking regions such as Brittany for its slightly sweet flavor and long storage life, and gardeners choose it over rounder shallot types specifically for its distinctive shape and keeping quality.

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring or late summer; He-Shi-Ko clumps and regrows from the base, so a single sowing can be harvested repeatedly.

directions: He-Shi-Ko is a traditional Japanese heirloom bunching onion that never forms a bulb, instead sending up tall, slender, silvery-white stalks that clump and multiply from the base as the plant matures. Sow thickly in rows and thin gradually, harvesting the largest stalks first and letting the remaining plants continue dividing for a repeated, cut-and-come-again supply through the season. Its mild, non-pungent flavor and tender texture make it a preferred variety for fresh eating raw or lightly cooked rather than for strong-flavored cooked onion dishes. He-Shi-Ko tolerates both cold and heat reasonably well, so gardeners often maintain a planting from early spring sowing through fall harvest without needing a second crop.

planting.note: Direct sow from early spring through midsummer for a succession of harvests into fall; Kyoto Market also overwinters well in milder climates.

directions: Kyoto Market is a vigorous, fast-growing Japanese bunching onion long associated with the traditional Kyo-yasai vegetables of the Kyoto region, prized for its long, straight white shanks and heavy, uniform yields. Sow seed directly and thin as stalks develop, harvesting young plants as slender scallions or letting them grow thicker without losing tenderness or flavor. Hilling soil around the base as the plants grow lengthens the blanched white portion for a more traditional Japanese-style leek-like scallion. Its disease resistance and tolerance of both heat and cold make Kyoto Market a reliable choice for extended-season plantings from spring through fall.
